claim: Genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors have revolutionized the study of signal transduction by enabling the real-time tracking of signaling activities in live cells.
source: Genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors have revolutionized the study of signal transduction by enabling the real-time tracking of signaling activities in live cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about the impact of biosensors on the field, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Investigating the interaction between signaling networks has become increasingly important to understanding complex cellular phenomena.
source: Investigating the interaction between signaling networks has become increasingly important to understanding complex cellular phenomena, necessitating an update of the biosensor toolkit to allow monitoring and perturbing multiple activities simultaneously in the same cell.
evidence: This reflects current trends and needs in the field of cell signaling research.

claim: A new class of fluorescent biosensors based on homo-FRET, called FLAREs (FLuorescence Anisotropy REporters), was developed.
source: We therefore developed a new class of fluorescent biosensors based on homo-FRET, deemed FLuorescence Anisotropy REporters (FLAREs), which combine the multiplexing ability of single-color sensors with a quantitative, ratiometric readout.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, describing the development of a new biosensor platform.

claim: FLAREs combine the multiplexing ability of single-color sensors with a quantitative, ratiometric readout.
source: We therefore developed a new class of fluorescent biosensors based on homo-FRET, deemed FLuorescence Anisotropy REporters (FLAREs), which combine the multiplexing ability of single-color sensors with a quantitative, ratiometric readout.
evidence: This describes the key features of the FLARE biosensors as demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Using an array of color variants, multiplexed imaging of three activity reporters simultaneously in the same cell was demonstrated.
source: Using an array of color variants, we were able to demonstrate multiplexed imaging of three activity reporters simultaneously in the same cell.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing co-expression and imaging of multiple FLARE sensors.

claim: FLAREs are compatible for use with optogenetic tools.
source: We further demonstrate the compatibility of FLAREs for use with optogenetic tools as well as intravital two-photon imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments combining FLAREs with channelrhodopsin.

claim: FLAREs are compatible for intravital two-photon imaging.
source: We further demonstrate the compatibility of FLAREs for use with optogenetic tools as well as intravital two-photon imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging experiments in mouse skeletal muscle.

claim: Single-color sensors with an intensiometric activity readout only occupy a single-color channel, allowing for more flexibility in multiplexed imaging experiments.
source: Single-color sensors, with an intensiometric activity readout, only occupy a single-color channel, allowing for more flexibility in multiplexed imaging experiments.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of single-color biosensors in the field.

claim: Single-color sensors are sensitive to variations in probe concentration caused by changing expression levels or cell shape.
source: However, they are sensitive to variations in probe concentration caused by changing expression levels or cell shape, as well as differences in imaging conditions, such as illumination intensity and focus.
evidence: This is a known limitation of intensiometric sensors.

claim: Single-color sensors are sensitive to differences in imaging conditions, such as illumination intensity and focus.
source: However, they are sensitive to variations in probe concentration caused by changing expression levels or cell shape, as well as differences in imaging conditions, such as illumination intensity and focus.
evidence: This is a known limitation of intensiometric sensors.

claim: Sensors with a ratiometric readout, such as those based on FRET, cancel out many variations in light intensity and probe concentration.
source: On the other hand, sensors with a ratiometric readout, such as those based on Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), cancel out many of these variations, enabling quantitative measurements of second messenger concentrations and better comparisons between experiments.
evidence: This is a known advantage of ratiometric FRET sensors.

claim: Ratiometric sensors enable quantitative measurements of second messenger concentrations and better comparisons between experiments.
source: On the other hand, sensors with a ratiometric readout, such as those based on Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), cancel out many of these variations, enabling quantitative measurements of second messenger concentrations and better comparisons between experiments.
evidence: This is a known advantage of ratiometric FRET sensors.

claim: The requirement for two distinct color channels in FRET sensors limits their application in multiplexed imaging.
source: However, the requirement for two distinct color channels limits their application in multiplexed imaging.
evidence: This is a known limitation of traditional FRET sensors.

claim: The loss of polarization of emitted light can be used as a readout for FRET between two fluorescent proteins.
source: Hence, rather than using the emission ratio between the FRET and donor channels, we instead used the loss of polarization of emitted light as a readout for FRET between two fluorescent proteins (FPs).
evidence: This describes the fundamental principle underlying FLARE sensors.

claim: The polarization-based FRET approach does not require the donor and acceptor to have distinct emission wavelengths.
source: Because this approach does not require the donor and acceptor to have distinct emission wavelengths, it can be used for either hetero-FRET (e.g. between different chromophores) or homo-FRET (e.g. between identical chromophores).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of using polarization rather than spectral separation.

claim: Homo-FRET measurements have been useful for detecting protein clustering and protein oligomerization in live cells.
source: Homo-FRET measurements have been useful for detecting protein clustering and protein oligomerization in live cells (Bader et al., 2011, Bader et al., 2009; Gautier et al., 2001), but only recently has the possibility of using homo-FRET in biosensor designs been explored (Warren et al., 2015; Cameron et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The possibility of using homo-FRET in biosensor designs has only recently been explored.
source: Homo-FRET measurements have been useful for detecting protein clustering and protein oligomerization in live cells (Bader et al., 2011, Bader et al., 2009; Gautier et al., 2001), but only recently has the possibility of using homo-FRET in biosensor designs been explored (Warren et al., 2015; Cameron et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: FLARE probes were created by adapting existing FRET-based biosensors for homo-FRET measurements by replacing the traditional FRET pair with two FPs of the same color.
source: To create our FLARE probes, we adapted existing FRET-based biosensors for homo-FRET measurements by replacing the traditional FRET pair with two FPs of the same color.
evidence: This describes the design strategy for creating FLARE sensors.

claim: FLARE biosensors include a molecular switch flanked by two spectrally similar FPs at the N- and C-termini.
source: The resulting biosensors include a molecular switch, which changes conformation in the presence of a particular biochemical activity, flanked by two spectrally similar FPs at the N- and C-termini.
evidence: This describes the structural design of FLARE sensors.

claim: Changes in the conformation of the molecular switch are monitored by observing the fluorescence anisotropy of the sensor using fluorescence polarization microscopy.
source: Changes in the conformation of the molecular switch, and thus the biochemical activities under study, are then monitored by observing the fluorescence anisotropy of the sensor using fluorescence polarization microscopy, with increased anisotropy corresponding to a lower-FRET state of the sensor, similar to the effect of increasing the intramolecular distance between the FRET pair (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the measurement method and is supported by figure data.

claim: Increased anisotropy corresponds to a lower-FRET state of the sensor.
source: Changes in the conformation of the molecular switch, and thus the biochemical activities under study, are then monitored by observing the fluorescence anisotropy of the sensor using fluorescence polarization microscopy, with increased anisotropy corresponding to a lower-FRET state of the sensor, similar to the effect of increasing the intramolecular distance between the FRET pair (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the relationship between anisotropy and FRET state.

claim: The molecular switch from AKAR4 is composed of an FHA1 domain and PKA substrate.
source: To develop a Protein Kinase A (PKA) activity FLARE, the molecular switch from A Kinase Activity Reporter 4 (AKAR4) (Zhang et al., 2001; Depry et al., 2011), composed of an FHA1 domain and PKA substrate (Figure 1a), was flanked between two FPs of the same color.
evidence: This describes the composition of the AKAR4 molecular switch, supported by citations.

claim: The FHA1 domain binds to the PKA substrate when the latter is phosphorylated.
source: The FHA1 domain binds to the PKA substrate when the latter is phosphorylated, altering the conformation of the molecular switch and leading to a change in FRET between the flanking homo-FRET pair.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the AKAR sensor.

claim: Phosphorylation of the PKA substrate alters the conformation of the molecular switch and leads to a change in FRET between the flanking homo-FRET pair.
source: The FHA1 domain binds to the PKA substrate when the latter is phosphorylated, altering the conformation of the molecular switch and leading to a change in FRET between the flanking homo-FRET pair.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the AKAR sensor.

claim: Two FLARE-AKAR variants based on mVenus were developed: one with a circularly permuted C-terminal FP (cp172Venus) and one without circular permutation.
source: To test the effect of FP circular permutation on these biosensors, we developed two FLARE-AKAR variants based on the yellow FP mVenus: one in which the C-terminal FP was circularly permuted at position 172 (cp172Venus), consistent with the hetero-FRET AKAR4 sensor, and one without circular permutation.
evidence: This describes the design of two sensor variants to test the effect of circular permutation.

claim: Following PKA activation with forskolin and IBMX, the anisotropy of mVenus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR decreased from 0.29 ± 0.003 to 0.26 ± 0.003, a decrease of 0.028 ± 0.001 (N = 44, p<0.0001).
source: Following PKA activation using a cocktail of 50 μM forskolin (Fsk), an adenylyl cyclase activator, and 100 μM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX), a general phosphodiesterase inhibitor, the anisotropy decreased from 0.29 ± 0.003 to 0.26 ± 0.003, a decrease of 0.028 ± 0.001 (N = 44, biological replicates, unpaired, two-tailed t-test, p<0.0001), with the kinetics of the decrease matching those observed with AKAR4 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result supported by data in figures.

claim: The kinetics of the anisotropy decrease in mVenus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR match those observed with AKAR4.
source: Following PKA activation using a cocktail of 50 μM forskolin (Fsk), an adenylyl cyclase activator, and 100 μM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX), a general phosphodiesterase inhibitor, the anisotropy decreased from 0.29 ± 0.003 to 0.26 ± 0.003, a decrease of 0.028 ± 0.001 (N = 44, biological replicates, unpaired, two-tailed t-test, p<0.0001), with the kinetics of the decrease matching those observed with AKAR4 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a comparison with the established AKAR4 sensor, supported by figure data.

claim: The yellow FLARE-AKAR variant without circular permutation showed slightly reduced changes in anisotropy upon stimulation with Fsk/IBMX.
source: The yellow variant without the circular-permutation in the C-terminal FP showed slightly reduced changes in anisotropy upon stimulation with Fsk/IBMX (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2c), consistent with previous
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by figure data.

claim: A slight positive correlation between intensity and anisotropy change was observed for Venus-cp172Venus FLARE AKAR.
source: We observed a slight positive correlation between intensity and anisotropy change for Venus-cp172Venus FLARE AKAR; however, the expression level does not significantly impact the reporting ability of these sensors in general (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by figure data.

claim: Expression level does not significantly impact the reporting ability of FLARE sensors in general.
source: We observed a slight positive correlation between intensity and anisotropy change for Venus-cp172Venus FLARE AKAR; however, the expression level does not significantly impact the reporting ability of these sensors in general (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing minimal correlation.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR was calculated to be 32.
source: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR was calculated to be 32 by dividing the magnitude of the anisotropy change upon maximal PKA stimulation by the standard deviation of the baseline before stimulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of sensor performance.

claim: PKA inhibition using H-89 led to an immediate slope change and increase in anisotropy in Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR.
source: PKA inhibition using 20 μM H-89 led to an immediate slope change and increase in anisotropy (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation demonstrating reversibility of the sensor response.

claim: A threonine-to-alanine (T-to-A) mutant version of FLARE-AKAR showed no change in anisotropy upon PKA stimulation with Fsk/IBMX or inhibition with H-89.
source: On the other hand, a mutant version of the biosensor with a threonine-to-alanine (T-to-A) mutation at the phosphorylation site showed no change in anisotropy upon PKA stimulation with Fsk/IBMX or inhibition with H-89 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the observed changes in anisotropy were due to phosphorylation of the PKA substrate.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating specificity of the sensor response.

claim: The observed changes in anisotropy in FLARE-AKAR were due to phosphorylation of the PKA substrate.
source: On the other hand, a mutant version of the biosensor with a threonine-to-alanine (T-to-A) mutation at the phosphorylation site showed no change in anisotropy upon PKA stimulation with Fsk/IBMX or inhibition with H-89 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the observed changes in anisotropy were due to phosphorylation of the PKA substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of response in the T-to-A mutant.

claim: Isoproterenol induced FLARE-AKAR responses in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, isoproterenol, a β-adrenergic agonist, induced FLARE-AKAR responses in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation demonstrating dose-response behavior.

claim: Mutation of the chromophore of the C-terminal cp172Venus in Venus-cp172Venus FLARE AKAR from GYG to GGG decreased the magnitude of the response to Fsk/IBMX to approximately one-third of that of the wild-type sensor.
source: To further demonstrate that the change in anisotropy upon PKA stimulation was due to a change in FRET, we mutated the chromophore of the C-terminal cp172Venus in Venus-cp172Venus FLARE AKAR from GYG to GGG. We observed that the magnitude of the response to Fsk/IBMX decreased to approximately one-third of that of the wild-type sensor (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an experimental result demonstrating the role of FRET in the sensor response.

claim: The remaining response in the chromophore-dead mutant was likely due to intermolecular FRET that occurs when the FHA1 domain of one molecule binds to the phosphorylated PKA substrate in an adjacent molecule.
source: The remaining response was likely due to intermolecular FRET that occurs when the FHA1 domain of one molecule binds to the phosphorylated PKA substrate in an adjacent molecule.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the residual response in the mutant.

claim: A panel of color variants of FLARE-AKAR was developed, including EGFP-EGFP, mCherry-mCherry, mCerulean3-mCerulean3, and mCerulean3-cp173Cerulean3 versions.
source: In addition to the yellow sensors, we developed a panel of color variants of FLARE-AKAR, including EGFP-EGFP, mCherry-mCherry, mCerulean3-mCerulean3 (Markwardt et al., 2011), and mCerulean3-cp173Cerulean3 versions.
evidence: This describes the development of multiple sensor variants.

claim: All color variants of FLARE-AKAR exhibited a decrease in anisotropy in cells treated with Fsk/IBMX.
source: All these variants exhibited a decrease in anisotropy in cells treated with Fsk/IBMX; however, the magnitude of the anisotropy decrease depended on the choice of FP, with the mVenus-cp172Venus variant having the largest response (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation across multiple sensor variants.

claim: The magnitude of the anisotropy decrease in FLARE-AKAR depended on the choice of fluorescent protein, with the mVenus-cp172Venus variant having the largest response.
source: All these variants exhibited a decrease in anisotropy in cells treated with Fsk/IBMX; however, the magnitude of the anisotropy decrease depended on the choice of FP, with the mVenus-cp172Venus variant having the largest response (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of different sensor variants.

claim: The Cerulean3-based FLARE-AKAR showed an increased dynamic range with a circularly permutated fluorescent protein at the C-terminal position.
source: As with the Venus variants, the Cerulean3-based FLARE-AKAR showed an increased dynamic range with a circularly permutated fluorescent protein at the C-terminal position.
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing variants with and without circular permutation.

claim: Changes in anisotropy in mCherry-mCherry FLARE-AKAR corresponded with the changes in normalized emission ratio in AKAR4, with similar kinetics.
source: mCherry-mCherry FLARE-AKAR, being spectrally shifted from the AKAR4 heteroFRET sensor allowed for direct comparison of FLARE and heteroFRET sensors within the same cell. As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6, changes in anisotropy in mCherry-mCherry FLARE-AKAR corresponded with the changes in normalized emission ratio in AKAR4, with similar kinetics.
evidence: This is a direct comparison between FLARE and traditional FRET sensors in the same cells.

claim: FLARE-AKAR sensors can monitor kinase activity at particular subcellular compartments.
source: We furthermore demonstrated the ability of FLARE-AKAR sensors to monitor kinase activity at particular subcellular compartments. By fusing Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR to targeting motifs from Lyn kinase and DAKAP1, we were able to detect PKA activity at the plasma membrane and outer mitochondrial membrane, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with subcellularly targeted sensors.

claim: Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR fused to Lyn kinase targeting motif can detect PKA activity at the plasma membrane.
source: By fusing Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR to targeting motifs from Lyn kinase and DAKAP1, we were able to detect PKA activity at the plasma membrane and outer mitochondrial membrane, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is an experimental demonstration of subcellular targeting.

claim: Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR fused to DAKAP1 targeting motif can detect PKA activity at the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: By fusing Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-AKAR to targeting motifs from Lyn kinase and DAKAP1, we were able to detect PKA activity at the plasma membrane and outer mitochondrial membrane, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is an experimental demonstration of subcellular targeting.

claim: PKA activity has slower kinetics and a lower magnitude in the nucleus than the cytosol in HeLa cells.
source: Moreover, we used untargeted FLARE sensors to detect differential PKA activity dynamics in different compartments; diffusable Venus-cp172Venus FLARE AKAR in HeLa showed that PKA activity has slower kinetics and a lower magnitude in the nucleus than the cytosol (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is an experimental observation of compartment-specific PKA dynamics.

claim: A family of single-color kinase activity or activation reporters in various colors was developed.
source: To demonstrate the generalizability of FLAREs, we developed a family of single-color kinase activity or activation reporters in various colors (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the expansion of the FLARE platform to multiple kinases.

claim: Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-EKAR-EV exhibited a decrease in anisotropy of 0.02 ± 0.001 (N = 13) after treatment with 100 ng/mL EGF.
source: When expressed in HEK293T cells, Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-EKAR-EV exhibited a decrease in anisotropy of 0.02 ± 0.001 (N = 13) after treatment with 100 ng/mL epidermal growth factor (EGF) to activate the MAPK pathway (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result for the EKAR sensor.

claim: The FLARE-EKAR-EV response was reversed upon MEK inhibition using U0126.
source: This response was reversed upon MEK inhibition using 20 μM U0126, and no change in anisotropy was observed with a T-to-A mutant sensor.
evidence: This demonstrates reversibility and specificity of the EKAR sensor.

claim: No change in anisotropy was observed in the T-to-A mutant of FLARE-EKAR-EV upon EGF stimulation.
source: This response was reversed upon MEK inhibition using 20 μM U0126, and no change in anisotropy was observed with a T-to-A mutant sensor.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating specificity.

claim: Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-CKAR exhibited an anisotropy decrease of 0.02 ± 0.001 (N = 26) upon activation of PKC with 100 ng/mL PMA.
source: Likewise, we developed a panel of PKC activity reporters, called FLARE-CKARs, by flanking a PKC sensor domain composed of an FHA1 domain and a PKC substrate (Herbst et al., 2011) from a CKAR2 construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) with mVenus-cp172Venus. We observed an anisotropy decrease of 0.02 ± 0.001 (N = 26) upon activation of PKC with 100 ng/mL phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result for the CKAR sensor.

claim: For FLARE-EKAR and FLARE-CKAR, sensors based on mVenus exhibited the largest responses.
source: For both FLARE-EKAR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and FLARE CKAR (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), we likewise repeated this process for various color variants, and like the FLARE-AKARs, the sensors based on mVenus exhibited the largest responses.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis across color variants.

claim: A myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) sensor was converted to a FLARE by exchanging the cyan FP for mVenus.
source: Furthermore, a myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) sensor was converted to a FLARE by exchanging the cyan FP for mVenus (Isotani et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the adaptation of an existing sensor to the FLARE format.

claim: Calmodulin association with the MLCK-CaM binding domain decreases FRET, leading to an increase in fluorescence anisotropy upon forced calcium entry with 30 mM KCl.
source: Calmodulin (CaM) association with the MLCK-CaM binding domain in between the FPs decreases FRET, leading to an increase in fluorescence anisotropy upon forced calcium (Ca2+) entry with 30 mM KCl (N = 13) (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the mechanism and experimental result for the MLCK sensor.

claim: FLAREs for monitoring second messenger dynamics were developed.
source: In addition to biosensors for monitoring enzymes, we also developed FLAREs for monitoring second messenger dynamics (Figure 3a).
evidence: This describes the expansion of FLAREs to second messenger detection.

claim: Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-Cameleon exhibited a decrease in anisotropy of 0.03 ± 0.002 (N = 10) upon addition of 1 μM ionomycin and 5 mM CaCl2.
source: When expressed in HEK293T cells, Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-Cameleon exhibited a decrease in anisotropy of 0.03 ± 0.002 (N = 10) upon addition of 1 μM ionomycin and 5 mM CaCl2, with the Venus-Venus, mCerulean3-mCerulean3, and mCherry-mCherry versions also showing detectable responses (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result for the calcium sensor.

claim: Venus-Venus, mCerulean3-mCerulean3, and mCherry-mCherry versions of FLARE-Cameleon showed detectable responses to calcium.
source: When expressed in HEK293T cells, Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-Cameleon exhibited a decrease in anisotropy of 0.03 ± 0.002 (N = 10) upon addition of 1 μM ionomycin and 5 mM CaCl2, with the Venus-Venus, mCerulean3-mCerulean3, and mCherry-mCherry versions also showing detectable responses (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation across color variants.

claim: mVenus-based FLARE sensors tend to show larger dynamic ranges for a variety of FLARE sensors than mCerulean3 or mCherry variants.
source: The mVenus-based FLARE sensors tend to show larger dynamic ranges for a variety of
evidence: This is a general observation across multiple sensor types.

claim: The superior performance of mVenus-based FLAREs is likely due to the superior extinction coefficient and quantum yield of mVenus, which make it a good FRET donor and acceptor.
source: FLARE sensors than mCerulean3 or mCherry variants, likely due to the superior extinction coefficient and quantum yield of mVenus, which make it a good FRET donor and acceptor.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of mVenus.

claim: Venus-cp172Venus FLARE Cameleon can detect submaximal calcium responses in histamine-stimulated HeLa cells.
source: We further demonstrated the ability of Venus-cp172Venus FLARE Cameleon to detect submaximal responses by monitoring calcium transients in histamine-stimulated HeLa cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This demonstrates the sensitivity of the sensor to physiological stimuli.

claim: The dissociation constant and Hill coefficients of purified Venus-cp172Venus Cameleon are in good agreement with other Cameleon sensors.
source: In order to determine the dissociation constant and Hill coefficients, we purified Venus-cp172Venus Cameleon and measured the fluorescence anisotropy in solutions of known free Ca2+ concentration at different temperatures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The resulting parameters are in good agreement with other Cameleon sensors (Nagai et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison with established sensors, supported by citation.

claim: A calcium FLARE sensor based on D1-ER was developed with a sensitivity appropriate for calcium monitoring in the ER.
source: Furthermore, we developed another calcium FLARE sensor, based on D1-ER (Palmer et al., 2004), with a sensitivity appropriate for calcium monitoring in the ER.
evidence: This describes the development of an ER-targeted calcium sensor.

claim: The D1-ER FLARE sensor anisotropy decreases upon increasing calcium concentration and increases when calcium is depleted from the ER upon treatment with thapsigargin.
source: The anisotropy decreases upon increasing calcium concentration and increases when calcium is depleted from the ER upon treatment with thapsigargin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the response characteristics of the ER calcium sensor.

claim: The fluorescence anisotropy of Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-ICUE increased by 0.02 ± 0.001 (N = 40) upon stimulation with Fsk/IBMX.
source: When expressed in HEK293T cells, the fluorescence anisotropy of Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-ICUE increased by 0.02 ± 0.001 (N = 40) upon stimulation with Fsk/IBMX (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result for the cAMP sensor.

claim: FLAREs only occupy a single-color channel.
source: The fact that FLAREs only occupy a single-color channel and are highly generalizable for different biosensors, as well as color variants, highlights their utility for multiplexed imaging applications.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of FLARE sensors.

claim: FLAREs are highly generalizable for different biosensors and color variants.
source: The fact that FLAREs only occupy a single-color channel and are highly generalizable for different biosensors, as well as color variants, highlights their utility for multiplexed imaging applications.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the development of multiple sensor types and color variants.

claim: Multiplexing of hetero-FRET sensors is generally limited to two probes.
source: While multiplexing of hetero-FRET sensors is generally limited to two probes (Depry et al., 2013; Shcherbakova et al., 2012), we demonstrate that FLAREs can facilitate co-imaging of three biosensors simultaneously.
evidence: This is a known limitation of traditional FRET sensors, supported by citations.

claim: FLAREs can facilitate co-imaging of three biosensors simultaneously.
source: While multiplexing of hetero-FRET sensors is generally limited to two probes (Depry et al., 2013; Shcherbakova et al., 2012), we demonstrate that FLAREs can facilitate co-imaging of three biosensors simultaneously.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the triple-sensor imaging experiment.

claim: Clear and distinct decreases in anisotropy were observed in the red channel after Fsk/IBMX treatment, in the yellow channel after EGF stimulation, and in the cyan channel after thapsigargin treatment in cells co-expressing three FLARE sensors.
source: We co-expressed mCherry-mCherry FLARE-AKAR, Venus-cpVenus FLARE-EKAR-EV, and mCerulean3-mCerulean3 FLARE-Cameleon in HEK293T cells and acquired a time-course with sequential treatment using Fsk/IBMX, EGF, and thapsigargin. Clear and distinct decreases in anisotropy were observed in the red channel after Fsk/IBMX treatment, in the yellow channel after EGF stimulation, and in the cyan channel after thapsigargin treatment, corresponding to an increase in PKA activity, Erk activity, and intracellular Ca2+, respectively (N = 17) (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is the key experimental result demonstrating three-color multiplexing.

claim: The anisotropy changes in the triple-sensor experiment corresponded to an increase in PKA activity, Erk activity, and intracellular Ca2+, respectively.
source: Clear and distinct decreases in anisotropy were observed in the red channel after Fsk/IBMX treatment, in the yellow channel after EGF stimulation, and in the cyan channel after thapsigargin treatment, corresponding to an increase in PKA activity, Erk activity, and intracellular Ca2+, respectively (N = 17) (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This interprets the anisotropy changes in terms of the biological activities being measured.

claim: MIN6 β-cells transfected with Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-ICUE and mCerulean3-mCerulean3 FLARE-Cameleon showed clear fluorescence anisotropy oscillations in both channels following stimulation with TEA.
source: MIN6 β-cells were transiently transfected with Venus-cp172Venus FLARE-ICUE and mCerulean3-mCerulean3 FLARE-Cameleon to simultaneously monitor cAMP and Ca2+ ﻿dynamics, respectively (N = 19). We observed clear fluorescence anisotropy oscillations in both channels following stimulation with 20 mM tetraethylammonium chloride (TEA) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This demonstrates the ability to monitor oscillatory dynamics with FLAREs.

claim: Ca2+ and cAMP exhibit synchronized oscillations in MIN6 cells, with Ca2+ increases corresponding to cAMP decreases.
source: Ca2+ and cAMP exhibit synchronized oscillations, with Ca2+ increases corresponding to cAMP decreases, consistent with previous findings (Landa et al., 2005; Ni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an experimental observation consistent with previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Even the lower signal mCerulean3-based FLARE sensors can be used under sub-maximal and physiologically relevant stimulation conditions in multiplexed imaging experiments.
source: These data demonstrate that even the lower signal mCerulean3-based FLARE sensors can be used under sub-maximal and physiologically relevant stimulation conditions in multiplexed imaging experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MIN6 cell experiments.

claim: FLARE sensors can be used simultaneously with optogenetic tools to perturb and monitor biochemical activities.
source: In addition to multiplexed biosensor imaging, the fact that FLARE sensors occupy only a single color channel also permits simultaneously perturbing and monitoring biochemical activities using optogenetics and FLAREs, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the channelrhodopsin experiment.

claim: Illumination with blue light of REF52 cells co-expressing mCherry-tagged hChR2 and Venus-cp172 FLARE-Cameleon produced an immediate decrease in anisotropy, corresponding to an increase in intracellular Ca2+.
source: We coexpressed an mCherry-tagged, ER-targeted channelrhodopsin2 (hChR2) (Nagel et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2009; Markwardt et al., 2016), a light-gated calcium ion channel, with Venus-cp172 FLARE-Cameleon in REF52 cells, a rat embryonic fibroblast cell line. Illumination with blue light produced an immediate decrease in anisotropy, corresponding to an increase in intracellular Ca2+ (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This demonstrates optogenetic control combined with FLARE imaging.
